passages.title: What makes a masterpiece?
passages.text: What makes a work of art a masterpiece? It is tempting to answer that it is simply a question of talent, but the history of art suggests otherwise. Many paintings that are now considered masterpieces were ignored or even ridiculed when they were first shown. What changed was not the paintings themselves but the way people looked at them. Critics, collectors and museums all play a role in deciding which works are remembered and which are forgotten. That said, a work does not become a classic by accident. The pieces that stand the test of time tend to share certain qualities: they are thought-provoking, they reward a second or third look, and they speak to experiences that every generation recognizes. It is this ability to stay relevant, rather than technical perfection, that distinguishes a great work from a merely good one. Some masterpieces are also an acquired taste. A first encounter with abstract painting or experimental music can be confusing, even irritating. What many people discover, however, is that the confusion is part of the experience, and that understanding comes with time.

passages.title: Who owns culture?
passages.text: Should museums return objects that were taken from other countries during the colonial era? For decades, the answer from most major institutions was a firm no. They argued that these collections were part of a shared world heritage and that the objects were better protected in their galleries than they would have been elsewhere. In recent years, however, that position has become harder to defend. Not only have governments formally requested the return of specific pieces, but researchers have also shown the way in which many of them were acquired: often by force, or for a fraction of their value. Critics point out that if these objects had stayed where they were made, local communities would now have direct access to their own cultural heritage. Some museums have begun to respond. A number of critically acclaimed exhibitions have been organized jointly with the countries of origin, and several institutions have returned items permanently. Others prefer long-term loans, which allow the objects to travel without settling the question of ownership. Whatever the solution, it is clear that the debate will not go away.
